entry.title: When 4-bit quantization uses more memory than bf16

link.title: When 4-bit quantization uses more memory than bf16

entry.content:
I expected quantizing SmolVLA’s backbone to save memory across the board. It didn’t.

Setup: SmolVLM2-500M backbone with LoRA, ARD dual action heads, and gradient checkpointing. The input was a bimanual action chunk of 50 steps. I measured peak forward+backward GPU memory on Colab.

What happened

  • At small batch sizes (1–8), 4-bit and 8-bit quantization saved roughly 3–26% compared with bf16.
  • At large batch sizes (16–32), the savings disappeared. In some settings, 8-bit used 23% more memory than bf16.

Why

  • Quantization only shrinks the stored weights of the frozen backbone. As the batch grows, activations take up most of the memory instead.
  • bitsandbytes also dequantizes weights on every forward pass, which adds overhead. This is especially costly for 8-bit LLM.int8().

Takeaway: quantization pays off for small-batch, low-VRAM settings, which is exactly the on-device case. On a GPU that can already fit large batches, it brings little benefit or even costs memory.

entry.title: Role-aware LAC: anti-shake filtering for asymmetric arms

link.title: Role-aware LAC: anti-shake filtering for asymmetric arms

entry.content:
Co-VLA’s LAC

Co-VLA (June 2026) proposes several ideas for coordinated bimanual control. The part I focused on is LAC (Latent-Aware Controller), a training-free filter applied at inference time.

The easiest way to think about LAC is image stabilization for robot arms.

How it works

LAC splits each bimanual command into two parts:

  • a shared motion that both arms make together, and
  • a residual motion that each arm makes on its own.

It then asks whether the residual is meaningful or just jitter. Based on the answer, it decides at every step whether to follow the new command immediately or hold the previous motion and follow slowly.

It distinguishes three cases:

What the arms do Example LAC’s call Action
move together carrying a desk large shared motion execute as is
push in opposite directions holding a bottle and twisting off the cap intentional coordination keep it
shake independently hands trembling jitter smooth it out

The middle case is the key. When the two hands apply opposing forces, as in opening a bottle, LAC recognizes deliberate coordination and doesn’t filter it away.

Going one step further with arm roles

ARD-VLA assigns each arm a role from the start, so the filter can treat them differently:

  • The Stabilizer arm (holding the bottle) always suppresses jitter strongly and stays firm.
  • The Actuator arm (twisting the cap) responds quickly and follows the command as is during coordinated motion.

It’s like a person holding a nail steady with one hand while swinging a hammer with the other.

Implementation

The implementation reuses ARD-VLA’s existing structure. ARD-VLA builds each command as a base action plus a role-specific residual. I took those two terms out directly and used them as LAC’s shared motion and residual motion.

  • LAC sits at the point where commands are sent to the arms one step at a time (select_action()).
  • A single config option selects off / original LAC / role-aware LAC.
  • Gripper open/close commands pass through without filtering.

Status: implemented on the lac-inference branch and not yet connected to the 2.0 closed-loop path. It hasn’t been validated with real weights or in simulation.

Code and a detailed write-up: judangyee/ARD-VLA
entry.summary: Adapting Co-VLA's training-free action filter to ARD-VLA's stabilizer/actuator split

entry.title: ARD-VLA 2.0: closing the loop with a shared-backbone judge

link.title: ARD-VLA 2.0: closing the loop with a shared-backbone judge

entry.content:
The problem: the original model is open-loop

The first version of ARD-VLA only produces actions. It never checks whether a step succeeded. If a grasp slips or an insertion misses, the model doesn’t notice. It moves on to the next step from a failed state and has no way to retry.

So I upgraded it to judge success at every step and plan around failures.

Architecture: one backbone, three branches

The judge is inspired by Laya, a “System 1” model that outputs only success/failure probabilities instead of generating text. Running a second VLM backbone just for judging would be expensive, so I kept SmolVLA’s SmolVLM2 backbone and borrowed only Laya’s output format.

A single backbone pass reads the inputs once. Three branches share its features:

Branch Role Output
Judge head what to do calibrated success probability, one of 5 failure types, progress (0–1); no gradient into the backbone
Selector head what to do picks one allowed candidate: next step, a recovery, or stop
Action expert + ARD heads how to move 50-step action chunk via flow matching, split into Stabilizer (left arm) and Actuator (right arm)

The inputs are the camera image, an instruction (goal, current subtask, and completed steps), and the robot state (16 DoF: 7 joints + 1 gripper per arm).

On top sits a decision layer. It is a set of rules, not a trained module, and it outputs one of ADVANCE, RETRY, RECOVER, RECHECK, or STOP. That decision sets the next cycle’s instruction and whether the chunk gets executed. A safety rule restricts it to allowed candidates and stops the robot once a retry limit is exceeded.

One cycle

  1. Observe and build the instruction for the current node.
  2. Run one backbone forward pass, which produces the action chunk and the Judge/Selector outputs.
  3. If the previous subtask just ended, the decision layer acts:
    • RETRY: execute this chunk as is.
    • ADVANCE / RECOVER: the instruction changes, so observe again.
    • RECHECK: observe again without executing.
    • STOP: move to a safe pose and end.
  4. Otherwise, execute the chunk step by step until the subtask ends or its step budget runs out.

Judgment happens only after a subtask ends, based on what the robot observes after executing it. While a subtask is in progress, the cost is one forward pass per chunk. ADVANCE and RECOVER add one extra pass because the instruction changes. So “one backbone pass” holds per chunk; actual end-to-end latency still has to be measured with real weights.

Task planning in three layers

Layer When Who What it does
Task graph before execution a human (for fixed processes) or an LLM defines subtasks, their order, entry/exit conditions, allowed recoveries, and retry limits
In-execution selection after each subtask decision layer + Selector chooses the next node, a recovery, a recheck, or stop, but only among options the graph allows
Replanning after STOP a human or an LLM edits the graph itself from a safe pose (add steps, reorder, change recovery methods)

For example, a peg-in-hole graph is align → insert → done. Each step has recovery candidates:

  • R1: redo the same step
  • R2: return to the start pose
  • R3: retry with different settings

At first a rule table picks the recovery; later the trained Selector picks it from the scene. If the limit is exceeded, the robot executes R4 STOP: it holds a safe pose, and the graph is fixed one level up.

How this differs from existing approaches

Compared with Their limitation ARD-VLA 2.0
Open-loop VLAs (SmolVLA, OpenVLA, ARD-VLA v1) never check success; move on from failed states judges every step and retries the same step with a different method
LLM planner + VLA replanning mid-execution takes seconds; can hallucinate steps or break format judging and selection fit inside one backbone pass; nothing is generated, so no invented steps
Separate VLM success detector a second model adds memory and latency shares the policy’s backbone and adds only small heads, so it targets a single consumer GPU
Symmetric bimanual VLAs can’t tell which arm caused a failure judges right-arm failures and left-arm slips separately, carrying role asymmetry into judging

Caveat: these are design-level differences. The structure is implemented and passes tests with a tiny synthetic model, but it hasn’t been trained or measured with real weights yet. Running it in Isaac Sim is the next step once I have the hardware.
